FSEC members offered wide-ranging comments on the report.
A stated goal in the report was to significantly increase graduate enrollment but faculty are right to be skeptical about how this might come to pass.
Many departments have experienced declines in their full-time faculty lines and wonder where the resources will come from to support this increase.
Other suggestions, like eliminating the Graduate Council’s role in the course approval process seem to run counter to the long-standing principle of faculty involvement in curricular matters.
Assertions about “branding” also seem misguided as graduate programs tend to attract their students via college- or department- specific outreach and not through an overarching administrative unit.
A number of other practical considerations would seem to limit the report’s stated aspirations.
These include recent decreases and eliminations in federal funds (and unpredictable access to existing funds), and limits on international students’ ability to access programs.

There is also a lot of uncertainty around the university’s roll out of a new budget model and its proposal to create a medical school.
These works in progress make it difficult to gauge the potential success of the report’s recommendations.
Even mundane suggestions like updating admissions systems have little 2

chance of success if they are cost-prohibitive.
Having no sense of the resources that will be available for improving or expanding graduate education make it difficult, if not impossible, for faculty to comment meaningfully.
FS President Williams will contemplate the faculty senate’s role in responding to the report so that some specific guidance might be offered and the discussion will continue next time. 6.

NECHE reaccreditation was also discussed and the steering committee has developed a survey to be deployed as part of the kick-off of the self-study process.

Also discussed was complications related to allowing simultaneous cross-enrollment in the traditional 14-week calendar and the accelerated calendar.
Faculty are concerned about the implications for faculty lines as enrollments could increase without a corresponding increase in full-time faculty.
There have also been ongoing conversations about “required” syllabus statements which have become problematic for faculty and which stand to take attention away from actual course materials and other inclusions that are much more relevant to the average student.
Options like creating a web page - accessible via link or QR code - as a repository for all such statements.
